In this practical, we will be looking at three major components of the MGnify Proteins database:

- HMMER sequence search using the MGnify Proteins website
- The Protein Landing Pages for individual MGnify Proteins
- Programmatic access to the database

## MGnify Proteins website overview

First, go to the [MGnify Proteins website](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/metagenomics/proteins/), and let's look at its main page together first.

![**Figure 1.** The top part of the MGnify Proteins website main page. **A)** MGnify Protein sequences bear `MGYP` accessions, and it's possible to search for MGYPs of interest here. **B)** Information about the latest release can be found here, including the number of cluster representatives.](images/mgnify_proteins_website_top.png){width=100%}

Figure 1 shows the top part of the main page. There are two points of interest here:

- **A\)** A text box that allows you to input a known MGYP accession.
- **B\)** Information about the latest MGnify Proteins release.

### MGYP accessions

All non-redundant protein sequences within the database are accessioned as **MGYP**s. For example, `MGYP008002629865` corresponds to the unique sequence:

```
>MGYP008002629865
MEYKVLLTVFAAVFIAELGDKTQLATMLFAADKEVSKLTVFIGASFA
LIAASGMGVLAGGFISQYMSERHLQLIAGIGFIAIGIWTLFKALTSG
```

This non-redundant sequence can then potentially be found in more than one assembly. If so, both occurrences of that sequence would have the same MGYP accession.

We will come back to **A\)** later on in the practical, once we have some MGYPs of interest from running the HMMER sequence search.

### MGnify Proteins releases

The latest release of MGnify Proteins is from July 2026, and so its release name is `2026_07`. The release consists of **5,739,566,171 MGYPs**, however the MGnify Proteins website only supports the **MGnify90** cluster representatives, which is a smaller, but still substantial, subset of **1,661,142,385 MGYPs**, which is what can be seen in **B\)**.

There are ways of accessing the full dataset programmatically, which we will look at in a later section.
